articles.title: 12 Christmas scams to watch out for
articles.summary: Here are the commonly launched scams this holiday season

items: The Philippine National Police (PNP) warns the public about various scams prevalent during the Christmas season, including smishing, vishing, and quishing.
Common tactics used by scammers include impersonating trusted entities, using fake QR codes, and offering too-good-to-be-true deals to steal sensitive information.
The PNP advises consumers to verify sellers, avoid sharing personal information, and be cautious of unsolicited messages and offers.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Christmas is right around the corner, and so are scams. The Philippine National Police (PNP) cautioned the public to be wary of their online transactions and the notifications they receive.

The PNP stressed the importance of verifying the legitimacy of sellers and the products and services they are offering. But scams aren’t just in online shopping anymore; they are in text messages, calls, and even in everyday physical stores.
Here are the usual scams and their tactics to look out for this Christmas.

Smishing is phishing, but through text messages. Attackers use portable International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) catchers to spoof the sender ID of legitimate banks, digital wallets, and government agencies.
This device acts like a fake cell tower, blasting messages to devices that connect to its signal. Since it can spoof the sender ID, the messages may appear in existing conversations.

These messages often include links that lead users to a spoofed website with a premise that you have a reward, a deadline to meet, or that your account is at risk of hacking. They ask for your information, passwords, and sometimes, one-time PINs (OTPs). Once given, attackers can make unauthorized transactions.

In 2022, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) released BSP Memorandum No. M-2022-015, requiring financial institutions not to include links in their messages and emails. Government agencies and financial institutions also send messages reminding consumers to never interact with links in text messages.

Voice phishing, or vishing, uses calls or voice messages to imitate trusted entities and trick victims into revealing sensitive information, according to the BSP. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) says scammers introduce themselves as a bank, digital wallet, or government agency personnel.

They use the same tactics as other forms of phishing. They conduct “verification procedures” by asking for your information and OTP, which banks and government agencies consistently remind customers to never share.
The rise of e-wallets and digital banking has allowed users to pay through QR codes. However, the BSP began warning the public about QR code fraud, or quishing.

In this case, fraudsters use QR codes to steal money and sensitive information from unsuspecting users. The code leads to fake login pages for e-wallets or banks, automatically downloads harmful content, or transfers money to unknown recipients.
QR codes usually don’t show website links. This makes it difficult for users to check.
The BSP warned users to be cautious and scan QR codes from verified stores. It added that most smartphones display the link before opening the webpage, which can help in verifying the site.
The institution also warned that attackers may alter or tamper with stores’ QR codes, placing a different code over legitimate ones.
This is the most frequent online scam. PNP chief General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., at a press briefing on November 9, said people should be skeptical of offers that seem too good to be true.
The PNP also reminds people to verify the seller’s credibility, keep communication on the same platform, and never share sensitive information.

Similar to fake online sellers, fraudsters offer unusually cheap tickets, booking deals, and vacation packages. This also leads users to phishing sites, allowing attackers to steal information and make unauthorized transactions.
Scammers pose as government agencies, such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), and spread links to surveys or registration to receive cash aid or gifts.
Though the department now offers digital payouts, it does not offer an open online application portal or form. Similarly, these fake portals are often phishing sites.

Investment frauds travel faster on social media because of Filipinos’ high usage. It depends on a “trust” mechanism and referrals, allowing users to transact or cooperate with people online with assurance.
Cryptocurrency is also used to lure victims with the promise of high yields.

In the 2026 book The Rogue Compound, these platforms use a “pump-and-dump” scheme where fraudsters artificially inflate the currency’s price and spread false hype to sell their shares. Once people invest, the price crashes, leaving investors with heavy losses.
Fraudsters also use charities, donation drives, and generosity to steal money. This does not only happen during disasters. The CICC included this scam in its list last year.

The PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group (ACG) advises users to verify the organization before donating, check official announcements, verified social media pages, and official bank accounts, and be wary of personal accounts soliciting donations and vague or unverifiable details.
Also known as “hijack profile scam.” This happens when scammers gain unauthorized access to social media accounts and message contacts, asking for urgent financial assistance.
Oftentimes, attackers gain access through phishing, hacking, or social engineering techniques. Hackers can also get banking details from those accounts, leading to unauthorized transactions.
Apart from smishing scams telling users that they won in a giveaway, this scam is also prevalent on social media.

The PNP says the usual red flags of these messages is you’re told you won a prize you never registered, asks for sensitive information, pressures you to act immediately, or instructed to make a transaction of investment.

The Rogue Compound book also explained how online gambling lures users through its architecture. According to one source, it operates in a “God-mode panel,” where operators configure the game’s parameters to tailor the user’s experience.

It tricks players into thinking they’re playing fairly by fluctuating between two settings: Newbie Setting and Kill Mode. The Newbie Setting tricks new accounts and first-time depositors by designing early wins to boost their confidence. Kill Mode activates when the victim keeps depositing money despite their losses.
The book also states that the scam only needs people who look for a quick source of income. “Receptionists” send messages at random on platforms such as Telegram, Viber, or WhatsApp.

It begins by instructing victims to do basic tasks for low-value commissions they can withdraw, which range from P100 to P200. They then instruct victims to deposit a small amount to gain access to an online platform that assigns them tasks. There, the cycle begins, helping establish trust.
Once the user makes bigger investments, the operators will demand more payment for various reasons before disappearing with the invested money. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt
articles.summary:
Travelers and crew feeling ‘pissed’ or ‘lucky’ depending on level of upset amid nationwide ground stop

The US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw…

blocks.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country, as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo.
At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded.
Steve Honberger, heading home to Portland, Oregon, with his wife and daughter, said he’d been on a plane about to take off when the shutdown was announced.
“They didn’t seem to know what’s happening, and they wanted to hold off as long as possible,” Honberger said. The plane sat at the gate for an hour and 40 minutes.

blocks.caption: Passengers inside an airplane at JFK airport in New York City on Friday. Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Reuters

blocks.text: They realized they were just going to be sitting at the gate, so they eventually asked to deplane and rebook.

Many still thought it worth showing up despite the uncertainty of when flights would resume. Rashid Kahn, heading for Miami, said he’d “heard about the ground stop on the news, but the airline said we might take off 10 or 11pm”.
“I am hopeful,” he added. “But maybe it’s something to do with the date. I’m not super serious, but it’s Friday the 13th.”

Tom Rolenaitis, returning a Shiba Inu show dog named Tsuki to Finland, said it was frustrating. “It’s cutting into a three-day trip and I have to get him back to his owner. We have no idea what’s happening.”

A flight attendant headed for Barcelona, who declined to give his name, said he had been told his American Airlines flight would be slightly delayed and all incoming international flights were being allowed to land.
Another crew member from the flight said cheerfully: “Things happen. Hopefully it will all be resolved.”

As the day wore on, passengers on international flights began to be boarding, prompting applause to erupt at the gates. “It’s moving, so that’s good,” said an airline representative. “But only international is going.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, citing a communications problems at regional air traffic control centers, according to an FAA notice. Four hours later, FAA sent out an advisory lifting the stop.

blocks.caption: Planes parked on the tarmac at JFK airport on Friday. Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Reuters

blocks.text: “You can’t moan about this kind of thing ... it’s such a first-world problem,” said Laura, a woman who lives in New York and was heading for San Francisco when her JetBlue flight was grounded. She still hoped her flight would go. “That what I have to figure out,” she said, sitting on the floor of the terminal.

With the lifting of the ground stop, more chaos followed. “My flight was cancelled, then I go to a kiosk, put my information in and it says I’m leaving at 3am. Then I talk to the desk and they know nothing,” said Larson Welsh, heading to Las Vegas from Paris.

The outage has nonetheless caused upheaval for thousands of passengers. There have been 10,343 flight delays within, into or out of the US so far, according to the website FlightAware, and 1,479 cancellations. More than 1,000 aircraft were bound for US when the ground stop was announced, according to Flightradar24.
Only two national ground stops have previously been issued: on 11 September 2001, after the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center; and in January 2023, after a communications failure.

The ground stop also snarled the sports world, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations before a big weekend of games. It also was unclear whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would make it on time.

blocks.caption: Travelers at JFK airport on Friday. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: Back at JFK, travelers expressed frustration and resignation.

“My flight to California was cancelled with no information and no rebooking. My flight was cancelled last night as well due to bad weather. Now I’m missing a family event,” said a man who gave his name only as Andy. “It’s frustrating. And I’m pissed.”
Honberger, meanwhile, tried to stay optimistic, saying: “There are people sitting on tarmac, so we count ourselves lucky and we were able to book ourselves a hotel for the night.”
Tom Johnson and agencies contributed reporting

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starship rocket, fails to recover booster
articles.summary: SpaceX had planned to catch and reuse both stages of its biggest rocket for the first time. But the booster exploded over the Gulf of Mexico, while the spacecraft continued into orbit.

image.caption: Fingers crossed that Saturday's landing of the top part of the rocket won't end like the boosterImage: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP

blocks.text: US company SpaceX has successfully launched the latest flight of its Starship spacecraft into orbit but did not recover the booster rocket as planned.
The company, owned by tech billionaire Elon Musk, is hoping to develop a fully reusable rocket system. It had planned to recover both the booster and the upper stage, which is the spacecraft itself.
Instead of landing back at the launch site, the booster exploded above the Gulf of Mexico. The upper stage is currently in orbitand the plan is to recover it on Saturday when it returns to Earth.
It is to be caught by mechanical arms upon landing back at the launch pad, marking the first time the spacecraft would return to Earth. It could then potentially be reused in the future.
In addition to testing the reusable rocket system, the mission also delivered 26 of SpaceX’s satellitesfor its Starlink network.
How did the launch go?

SpaceX's Starship is the world's largest and most powerful rocket system. At 124 meters (407 feet) tall, it consists of a spacecraft mounted on a booster rocket. Both stages were designed from the outset to be fully reusable.

At the launch, both the spacecraft and booster successfully lifted off from the SpaceX South Texas Starbase site. While the Friday launch was an uncrewed mission, Starship is designed to carry both crew and cargo.

blocks.caption: Both booster and Starship at the launch of the missionImage: Steve Nesius/REUTERS

blocks.text: On its return path, the booster diverted from its flight path to the launch site and steered to a designated area over the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded over the sea surface. The reasons for the failure of the controlled landing were not immediately clear.
"Not sure right now why we weren't able to bring it back," SpaceX's Dan Huot said.
The upper stage continued into orbit and soon after began releasing the 26 satellites it was carrying.
It is scheduled to return to Earth on Saturday.
Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX’s goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.

In previous launches, the Starship booster was successfully recovered. The upper stages of the 14 previous Starship missions have all ended up in the ocean though, either by design or because of failures.
The new objective of Friday’s launch was to recover both stages of the Starship launch system.
Currently, SpaceX is mostly using smaller Falcon rockets, which are not fully reusable because the second stage cannot be recovered.
Musk said he expected SpaceX to conduct Starship launches once a week by early 2027.
The project has received billions of dollars in NASA funding, with SpaceX also investing at least $15 billion.

articles.title: What we know about Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang
articles.summary: Alice Huang had a long career in Chinese finance before later emerging as an executive in the global race for artificial-intelligence chips.
articles.byline: WEN-YEE LEE, ANDREW SILVER, LAURIE CHEN, Reuters

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 10:23am
Alice Huang had a long career in Chinese finance before later emerging as an executive in the global race for artificial-intelligence chips.

Known also as Huang Le, she was a top executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that was an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region. Her reported affair with Jensen Huang led in part to his resignation as Nvidia CEO on November 12.

Several news organizations, including the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, have reported that US and other government authorities had suspicions that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing. In the spring of 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a classified memo detailing intelligence indicating that China's Ministry of State Security had recruited Huang to target Nvidia's CEO, the New York Times said.
Reuters has not been able to verify any of the allegations made in the New York Times, along with other media reports, about Huang's suspected spying for China.
Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy. Reuters attempts to reach Alice Huang have been unsuccessful. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.
Here are more details about what is known about Alice Huang:
Suspicions of spying, government statements

The New York Times reported on November 10 that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed President Donald Trump aboard Air Force One en ​route to China in May about US intelligence indicating Jensen Huang was involved with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

The briefing marked at least the second time in seven months that Trump had been told about the intelligence, the Times ​reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter. Reuters was not able to confirm these warnings to Trump.

President Trump said on November 9 that the FBI was looking into the spying allegations. He said Jensen Huang told him he had no idea of the spying allegations, and also said he did not need to act on intelligence when he was briefed.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on November 12 that the Department of Justice had not yet reached a conclusion as to whether Alice Huang was a spy for China. CNN reported that day that US intelligence officials are still working to understand their relationship, citing people who say there is disagreement about the strength of the evidence that she was recruited to spy for Beijing.

Singapore's home affairs ministry said on November 12 that it had seized Alice Huang's passport in 2025 while investigating her for other offenses, including buying servers that were exported via Singapore to Malaysia without entering the Singapore market. The ministry said there was insufficient evidence to establish Alice Huang had committed any offenses.

The country's foreign ministry also said it received "limited" help from the US in its probe that began in 2025 into false declarations in the purchase of servers and other related offenses. Alice Huang left the country in February and was barred from re-entering following Singapore's investigation, the ministry said.
Ties to Jensen Huang

The Financial Times reported on November 6 that Alice Huang had a romantic affair with Jensen Huang. On November 8, Jensen Huang released a statement acknowledging an extramarital affair, without naming Alice Huang in the statement.
Reuters has verified photos of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang together at several different events over the last two-plus years, with the earliest dating to December 2023.
Role at Megaspeed

Huang became the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed International in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records.

In October 2025, the New York Times reported the company was under US investigation over whether it was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export controls. China has denied this allegation, and there has been no public finding that Megaspeed violated ​the rules.
Earlier this week, The Information reported that Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip sales to China.
Megaspeed said on November 12 that it has cooperated with US inspections.
Corporate roles

Alice Huang previously worked in banking and investment management, according to Chinese fund-industry records and an indexed profile on private-fund database ​Simuwang, which also listed an earlier career in television journalism. She also held senior positions at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, a Chinese investment firm.
She held senior roles ​at a Shanghai investment firm before her role at Megaspeed, according to financial records, corporate filings and company materials reviewed by Reuters. — Reuters

articles.title: US lifts nationwide ground stop for airports hours after halting all departures
articles.summary: The US federal aviation regulator has lifted a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Trump administration officials blame "overloaded" and "outdated" systems for the hourslong halt to departures.

image.caption: Flights were delayed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, which serves the nation's capital Image: Jonathan Ernst/REUTERS

blocks.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) canceled a ground stop on all national flights hours after stopping departures at US airports on Friday.
"We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s old copper lines. We use an old system," US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. "It was a legacy network problem."

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the communications breakdown resulted from a cyberattack or artificial intelligence and that the ⁠public ​was ​never ​in danger.

Over 4,500 flights were canceled Friday and about 700 for Saturday and over 10,000 flights within, into, or out of the United States were delayed, according to the FlightAware aviation tracker. With some 11,000 flights scheduled to depart from US airports after 4 p.m. local time (2200 UTC), more cancellations were expected, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
What do we know so far?
"All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice," the FAA had said earlier Friday.

The agency said the ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." The FAA cited a temporary telecommunication outage and said, "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis."
The agency said flights were halted "out of abundance of caution."
In a post on X, Duffy said the stop was due to a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
"FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," he wrote.

The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, Eurocontrol, said all flights departing for US airports from its 42 member states were suspended following a request from the FAA to deal with technical issues.
Canada implementing 'traffic management' measures at major airports

Canada's air navigation service provider, NAV Canada, said it is closely monitoring the US ground stop and later said, "It was implementing traffic management measures at Toronto Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver to safely manage traffic volumes."
"Travelers should expect delays and check with their airline. Our systems are operating normally," NAV Canada added.
Toronto Pearson Airport said flights between Toronto and the US have been impacted by the ground stop.
The FAA ground stop order came a day after Duffy asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System.

"This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers.
It's the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the FAA dealt with a system outage. Prior to that, the last ground stop was after the September 11, 2001 terror attacks.

MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board issued special permits to 372 passenger buses in anticipation of an influx of passengers traveling during the five-day long Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit break.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Saturday said jeepney drivers, whose routes were affected by security measures implemented for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Pasay City, were also given cash aid by the government.

In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB, DSWD spokesperson Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said "close to hundred" jeepney drivers serving the Baclaran-Divisoria route were among the beneficiaries of P10,000-cash aid for those affected by ASEAN preparations.
"Nasa 2,500 na ang nabigyan natin ng assistance. Ito 'yung mga eatery workers, vendors, sari-sari store owners, jeepney drivers na naapektuhan," Dumlao said.
The DSWD official said the agency began distributing P10,000 cash assistance and family food packs on Sunday, November 8, 2026.

"Inumpisahan natin nu'ng Sunday sa may Diokno Boulevard. May mga eatery worker dun na naapektuhan. Nu'ng Wednesday, mayroon ding mga karagdagan pang eatery workers, sari-sari store owners at iba pang vendors sa may Pasay na tinulungan din natin," she said.

"Nu'ng Thursday, nasa Parañaque naman tayo. Nasa mahigit 1,400 na mga vendor, lalo na sa may Baclaran area ang nabigyan din ng assistance. Kahapon, bumalik tayo ng Pasay City... close to a thousand ang nabigyan din natin ng tulong-pinansyal," she added.
The DSWD has apologized to those affected by ASEAN security measures and preparations.

"We have worked with the local government units kaya naging mabilis ang provision ng assistance. Batid naman kasi ng pamahalaan na ang pagkakaantala ng kabuhayan ay talagang nakakapagdulot ng krisis sa pamilya," Dumlao said.

articles.title: All passengers and crew accounted for after New Orleans boat crash in ‘miracle on the Mississippi’
articles.summary: No passengers or crew were killed or critically hurt after a tanker collided with a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River, officials say
articles.byline: Ramon Antonio Vargas and Lucy Campbell in New Orleans

blocks.text: In what the city’s mayor declared a “miracle on the Mississippi”, all passengers were accounted for – with none killed or critically hurt – after a tanker collided with a river cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon.

Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’s American Heritage at about 12.30pm – but none of their injuries were considered critical, New Orleans’s mayor, Helena Moreno, said at a news conference.

Zero passengers or crew members were unaccounted for, Moreno said. She attributed that fact to a hectic but effective multi-agency rescue effort after the American Heritage was struck and a number of people ended up in the river, whose waters are cold and its currents are infamously perilous.
That “truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said near the scene of the crash, as a group of fellow officials around her applauded.
The American Heritage had 197 passengers onboard when it was hit, Port of New Orleans press secretary Kimberly Curth said in a statement.
About two hours before that, the American Heritage had docked at the port to begin passenger disembarkation, Curth said.

Thirty of those reported injured were on the American Heritage, and they were said to have mostly had bumps and bruises. Two others were harbor police officers who were on the river boat after the crash participating in rescue efforts.

Officials did not immediately provide details about what caused the crash. Moreno said investigators would explore whether there was some loss of steering on the Atlantic Asphalt before it struck the American Heritage, as an emergency response source had said earlier – but that had not been immediately confirmed.

The website marinetraffic.com showed the Atlantic Asphalt’s path was seemingly uneventful as it went around the challenging Mississippi River bend near New Orleans’ Algiers Point neighborhood. It had just made it past the Crescent City Connection bridge linking New Orleans’ central business district and the community’s Algiers section when it began heading generally to its starboard – or right – side.

Video provided to Guardian reporting partner WWL Louisiana showed the Atlantic Asphalt then T-boned the side of the American Heritage. The cruise ship eventually slowly rolled on to its side where it was struck, according to the video, which the CBS affiliate obtained from Barry Kern, proprietor of Mardi Gras World, a tourist attraction near the scene of the crash.
One witness, Jamie Holford, told local NBC News affiliate WDSU that it took 15 minutes “from impact to where it rolled over”.
“Surreal,” Holford said. “That’s what that was.”

Maritime law expert Martin J Davies of New Orleans’ Tulane University told local Fox affiliate WVUE that the Atlantic Asphalt was fortunate to have not hit the Crescent City Connection, which could have endangered motorists on a two-span, cantilever, steel truss bridge that is estimated to carry about 160,000 cars daily.
“This is obviously a really bad incident,” Davies said. “But it could also have struck the bridge, which it didn’t.”

A video from WDSU showed crew members of a tugboat working to pull people in lifejackets or holding on to flotation rings out of the river. An emergency response that drew in firefighters, US Coast Guard helicopter and boat crews, as well as port and city police – among others – also helped pull out people who ended up in the water in plain view of cameras and eyewitnesses.

One image on social media showed people climbing on the side of the cruise boat – specifically, on stateroom balconies – after it was struck, with chairs and tables strewn about after it evidently took on water.

Blake Paterson, an independent New Orleans journalist, who publishes Perdido Street.News, interviewed 65-year-old American Heritage passenger Tamara Carrasco about what she saw at the time of the crash.

The retired Atlanta elementary school teacher told Paterson that she was dining on the first floor of the riverboat when she saw the tanker careering toward the American Heritage. The tanker dropped its anchor, and she could see its crew running away on its deck, according to what Carrasco told Paterson.

Carrasco began running to the other side of the river boat, but she was knocked to the ground when the tanker hit. She said water began pouring into the dining room, making her think it was “like the Titanic”.

An employee at the Ernest N Morial Convention Center next to the scene of Friday’s crash said she realized something was awry when she could see from her vantage point that the tip of the American Heritage was tilted. She then grasped the nature of situation when she heard desperate shrieks.

“People were screaming for help,” said the employee, who asked to not be named. She recalled how she and colleagues assembled wheelchairs, water and other items in case survivors would soon need them.
The American Heritage’s passengers were brought inside the New Orleans port’s administration building, next to the convention center.

At the news conference where officials then confirmed there were no casualties, Louisiana governor Jeff Landry echoed Moreno in invoking the term “miracle”, especially “when you think about the population that was on that cruise ship – and the ability for us to get them off and out of the water”.
“The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond,” Landry said. “There were challenges out there.”

With everyone accounted for, New Orleans’s US Coast Guard commander, Melanie Burnham, said the focus would shift to re-opening the river to traffic. It had been closed from mile markers 93 to 96 to facilitate rescue efforts.
US House majority leader Steve Scalise, a suburban New Orleans Republican, said on Friday that the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) would investigate the crash.

A statement from American Cruise Lines on Friday said “guests and crew were evacuated” from the American Heritage but did not elaborate. “We are deeply concerned for everyone involved,” the cruise operator’s statement added.

The American Heritage, a 300ft paddle-wheel ship, was built in 2015 and previously sailed as the Queen of the Mississippi. It has more than 80 staterooms and operates cruises on the Mississippi River, including ones which depart from New Orleans.

The Atlantic Asphalt is a oil tanker built in 2017 measuring approximately 160 meters in length and has a deadweight of 17,764 metric tons. It flies the flag of the Marshall Islands and is owned and commercially operated by Nave Shipping SA, a company registered in Liberia. Its maintenance, technical and safety operations are overseen by Singapore-based Thome Ship Management, according to online records.
The vessel, which had a next recorded destination for Singapore, does not appear on the international sanctions lists checked by maritime tracking services, including Magic Port.
However, it was previously fined C$7,800 by Canadian authorities for a violation of the Canada Shipping Act and related vessel pollution regulations.

The penalty, recorded on 11 August 2020, stemmed from an officer failing to properly carry out their duties while supervising a transfer operation aboard the oil tanker, according to the Canadian government.

To many in New Orleans, the crash involving the Atlantic Asphalt called to mind an episode nearby – nearly 30 years earlier – when a cargo ship struck a wharf adjacent to the city’s Riverwalk shopping center and Hilton Riverside hotel.

No deaths resulted from that case, which occurred on 14 December 1996 after the Liberian-registered Bright Field lost propulsion power, an NTSB report later said. But there were more than 60 injuries reported, including four which were considered serious.
Maya Yang contributed reporting

articles.title: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
articles.summary:
The former coalminer’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’ sparked wide criticism, but his party has shown no signs of dumping him

  • Get our

blocks.text: In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation leader upper house candidate Stuart Bonds launches into a speech against “mass” migration.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by non-white immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the GOAT, an acronym for the greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.
Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”
“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.
The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.
But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.
“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.
One Nation could ‘clean the deck’ in regions
The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.
“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.
“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”
after newsletter promotion

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.
And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.
Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.
“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”
The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.
“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.
The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.

Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.
But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preferences flows aren’t guaranteed.
But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.
“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.
“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines hosts the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits from November 15 to 18, bringing together Southeast Asian leaders, dialogue partners and representatives of international institutions to discuss regional and global concerns.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and other ASEAN leaders are set to convene at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City for the summit's plenary and retreat, where they will take stock of the Philippines' 2026 chairship and discuss key regional challenges.
The gathering comes as ASEAN marks its expansion to 11 member states following the formal admission of Timor-Leste in October 2025.
The Philippines is hosting the summit under the theme "Navigating Our Future, Together," with priorities centered on peace and security, economic prosperity and people empowerment.
The Related Summits on November 16 and 17 will bring ASEAN leaders together with counterparts from Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia and the United States.
The Philippines will also formally turn over the ASEAN chairship to Singapore on November 17.

articles.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global disruption that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
articles.summary:
Experts say outage exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.
Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.
“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.
Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.
“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.
The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.
“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.
Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.
Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.
after newsletter promotion
Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.
Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.
The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.
In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.
When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

articles.title: ASEAN unity faces test as energy crisis, regional conflicts loom over summit
articles.summary: Southeast Asian foreign ministers begin meetings in Manila on Saturday as the regional bloc seeks a coordinated response to surging energy costs, security tensions, and an approaching El Niño,…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 8:51am

MANILA — Southeast Asian foreign ministers begin meetings in Manila on Saturday as the regional bloc seeks a coordinated response to surging energy costs, security tensions, and an approaching El Niño, challenges Philippine President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has said demand collective action.

"Especially at a time when we face multiple crises, from rising oil prices to security concerns and the approaching El Niño, ASEAN needs to act as one," Marcos said ahead of the meetings, which the Philippines will chair. "It is very important that we are united and find plans and solutions to address these problems."

The meetings open a weekend of diplomacy culminating in the November 15 to 17 ASEAN summit, where ASEAN leaders will hold talks with counterparts from major powers including the United States, China and Japan, and discuss wide-ranging issues from the economic fallout from the Middle East conflict, Myanmar, the South China Sea to transboundary pollution.

The gathering comes as the Philippines and other import-dependent Southeast Asian economies grapple with higher fuel costs, which have squeezed households and businesses and added to inflation pressures. The crisis has also exposed the limits of regional energy security, with proposals for a shared oil stockpile still under study.
A summit on the Asia Zero Emission Community, a Japan-led framework that aims to achieve energy security, economic growth and decarbonisation at the same time, will also be held next week.

US President Donald Trump, who will be in Manila for the summit, said this week he was unlikely to order new military strikes on Iran after appeals from countries including Qatar. The comments offered some reassurance to energy markets, though the prospect of renewed military action and disruption to oil supplies remains a concern for fuel-importing countries.
For ordinary Filipinos, the impact of the conflict has been more immediate.
Ahead of the meetings, 50-year-old jeepney driver Lito Albino appealed to Trump to help end the conflict, saying ordinary workers were bearing the consequences of a war they had no part in.

He said the conflict involving Iran had forced him to work longer hours for less money, and with three children and household expenses to cover, higher fuel costs had made it increasingly difficult to support his family.
"No one truly wins in a war. It is the poor and marginalised people like us who suffer the most," Albino said.
Myanmar test
Myanmar will also test ASEAN's ability to maintain a common position on the crisis that has engulfed the country since the military seized power in 2021.

Leaders are expected to review the implementation of the bloc's five-point consensus, its main framework for addressing the crisis, Philippine foreign ministry spokesperson Dominic Xavier Imperial said at a press conference on Friday. Their decision will be reflected in a negotiated document to be issued after the summit.

The South China Sea will feature in discussions with China, with negotiations on a long-delayed Code of Conduct about 70% complete, Imperial said. He said the figure represented overall progress in negotiations, not the proportion of text agreed.

Beyond the diplomatic meetings, Trump's visit is expected to draw protests from workers, students and left-wing groups, calling for an end to the Middle East conflict and the US-led Pax Silica to be scrapped.
Myanmar will also feature in protests planned during the summit, with activists demanding that ASEAN maintain its exclusion of coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing from leaders' meetings.

Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that the United Nations estimates has killed 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.

Hlaing's military has received support from China, India and Russia. His administration has gained increasing international recognition in recent months, with some ASEAN countries reengaging and US officials holding secret talks as the Trump administration reverses years of isolation. — Reuters

articles.title: Nationwide FAA ground stop: nearly 11,000 flights delayed or canceled at airports across the US
articles.summary: Transportation secretary said stoppage is due to ‘communication issue’ and homeland security says there’s no indication of ‘nefarious attack’

blocks.text: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights that are due to take off in the US on Friday, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware.

In a post on X, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the stoppage is due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter.
A notice from the FAA said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.
Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland security director, said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage do not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
“There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

blocks.caption: Departure flight screens at Chicago O’Hare international airport on Friday. Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: After restoring communications so all airborne flights can land, Mullin said, “we’re going to continue to work to find out what the root of the cause is”.
“We’re not ruling out anything at this point,” Mullin added.
Mullin said the immediate priority was ensuring that planes still in the air would be landing safely, but that there was no clear information on how long the stoppage might last.

In a statement, the Los Angeles mayor, Karen Bass, said that she was aware of the stoppage and receiving updates on it. Los Angeles is home to LAX, the fifth-busiest airport in the US, according to the bureau of transportation statistics.

“I am in close contact with leadership at Los Angeles World Airports (LAWA) to receive real-time updates and assess impacts. We will continue to monitor this evolving situation and work closely with federal and state partners.”

At Ronald Reagan Washington national airport, gate agents, along with most travelers in the terminal, refreshed their phones looking for updates, and attempted to change their flights. Nearly every seat was filled, with some people sitting on the floor and using their luggage as makeshift desks for their laptops.

blocks.caption: Boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport in Washington DC on Friday. Photograph: Zina Desmazes/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway airport and rippled across the rest of the US.
Amid the uncertainty, San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart.
John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.

A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air. This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 11 September 2001; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned.

blocks.caption: Stranded travelers at John F Kennedy international airport in New York City, New York, on Friday. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.
Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

articles.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
articles.summary: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.

blocks.text: ByVictoria Gill
Science correspondent
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'
Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.

Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
"He definitely feels lonely," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people

blocks.text: When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people

Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., external
Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.

"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."
King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.
"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo

blocks.text: Image source, Sinead Lynch/The Aspinall Foundation
Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo

African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.
But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.

In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.

It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.
"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.
"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response

blocks.text: Image source, G Forrester
Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response

Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.

The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.
And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".
But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.

No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.
Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.

These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.
The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events

blocks.text: Image source, Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund
Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events
The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.
"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.
And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.
"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives

blocks.text: Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives

Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."

Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."
But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.
Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.
"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."
That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.
"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.
"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

articles.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
articles.summary: The 52-year-old general’s provocative posts and military threats have fuelled rumours of a dynastic succession.

blocks.text: In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.

Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.

The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.

At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".

He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".

Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.
Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.

Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.

"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.
He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.
The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.
Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.
"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.
He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.
Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".

Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.
On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.
"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.
He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.
The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.
It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.
Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.

Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.
Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.
He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.
Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.
Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.
Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.
"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.
At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.
He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.
Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.
He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.
But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.
At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.
Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.
There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.
Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.

Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.
He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.
"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.
The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.

The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.
The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.
Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.
Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.
The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.
For now, Museveni remains in power.

But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.
