articles.title: Indonesia's wiretapping scandal opens a political fault line
articles.summary: Senior police officers are accused of illegally monitoring President Prabowo Subianto, exposing rival networks within Indonesia's security establishment and renewing concerns about political misuse…

image.caption: The surveillance allegedly targeted not just the president, but also ministries, lawmakers, students and others [FILE: September 13, 2026]Image: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: For decades, Indonesia's police and intelligence agencies have been accused of spying on politicians, journalists, and activists, Now, a widening scandal involving some of the country's most senior police officers has brought those concerns to the heart of government.
Earlier this month, Indonesian police named four senior officers as suspects in an alleged illegal surveillance operation targeting President Prabowo Subianto and other prominent figures.

Former national police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is not related to the president, was among the senior officers arrested. The ex-police chief became the president's chief of staff in October, just weeks before the scandal broke.
Investigators claim that officers intercepted communications without proper authorization in 2025 and 2026 and then tried to delete records of the operation.

Suyudi Ario Seto, the new police chief, told a parliamentary panel this week that the surveillance targeted the president, officials within the presidential palace, ministries, state institutions, lawmakers, political party figures, governors, anti-corruption officials, activists and students.

A parliamentary commission is investigating the motive behind the wiretapping operation and trying to uncover whether other senior figures were involved. Meanwhile, the police have opened an investigation into possible treason-related offenses.

blocks.caption: Following the wiretapping allegations, President Prabowo hosted ten former chiefs of the national police, along with current Police Chief Suyudi Ario Seto, at his residence for a goodwill meetingImage: Media Team of the President of the Republic of Indonesia

blocks.text: Intensifying political turmoil?
Amnesty International has called for investigations to also determine whether the wiretap operation was used to intimidate government critics and weaken civil liberties.

The government has responded by ordering an additional 20,000 troops to Jakarta as a precaution, although there had been no indication that the wiretap is part of a larger campaign intended to bring down Prabowo's administration.

The affair has intensified tensions between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo, commonly known as Jokowi, while exposing deeper problems with the powers and political loyalties of Indonesia's security establishment.
"The use of surveillance is actually pretty widespread," Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate professor at Universitas Jenderal Achmad Yani, told DW.
"While there are laws and regulations, they are flouted since there is no regulation on eavesdropping, especially by law enforcement agencies," he added.

Officially, Indonesia's Electronic Information and Transactions Law prohibits unauthorized interception, while other legislation permits surveillance for specified law enforcement and intelligence purposes.
Despite these safeguards against illegal interception, Sulaiman said it could be argued, "that the police and intelligence are essentially unconstrained."
A long history of surveillance
Indonesia's intelligence agencies and law enforcement have long played a role in political competition, Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.
Under Suharto's authoritarian New Order regime, which collapsed in 1998, intelligence agencies were central in monitoring political opponents and suppressing dissent.

After democratization, controversies persisted. In 1999, a leaked recording of a telephone conversation involving then-President BJ Habibie raised concerns about surveillance within the presidential palace itself.
In 2024, the elite counterterrorism unit, Densus 88, was caught surveilling Deputy Attorney General Febrie Adriansyah, who at the time was overseeing major corruption investigations.

But what makes the latest allegations particularly significant is "their apparent scale and the suggestion that surveillance capabilities may have been deployed outside established legal procedures and against the sitting president," Priyandita said.

blocks.caption: In 2024, former President Jokowi backed Prabowo's presidential campaign [FILE: November 9, 2023Image: Presidential Secretariat Press Bureau

blocks.text: A delicate moment for the leadership
Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo, a former special forces general, has sought to consolidate his authority over the country's political and security institutions.
Critics accuse him of accelerating the militarization of civilian government, including through legislation expanding the military's ability to occupy civilian posts.
However, the president inherited a security establishment partly shaped by his predecessor.
In 2024, Jokowi, who couldn't run for office again, backed Prabowo's presidential campaign and his eldest son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, became Prabowo's running mate and subsequently vice president.
The Jokowi-Prabowo alliance was decisive for Prabowo's electoral victory, but it also left him governing alongside officials and political networks cultivated during Jokowi's decade in power.
On Thursday, Jokowi's son Gibran resigned as vice president amid a growing controversy over his educational credentials.

Indonesia's Constitutional Court and the country's Supreme Court found that Gibran's overseas high school qualifications fell short of legal requirements for vice presidential candidates, and had been wrongly accepted by election authorities.
The academic credentials probe was apparently not related to the investigations into the wiretapping scandal.
Can Indonesia reform its security establishment?

A series of government reshuffles in recent months has also been interpreted as Prabowo's attempt to strengthen his control, especially against some Jokowi loyalists. Listyo, appointed police chief by Jokowi in 2021 and long regarded as close to the former president, was replaced in October.

"Prabowo may have consolidated his political authority since taking office, but that does not necessarily translate into complete control over institutions whose senior leadership and internal networks were shaped under the previous Jokowi government," Priyandita said.

Also, Prabowo may emerge politically stronger if the investigation weakens rival networks within the police. However, replacing one set of political loyalties with another would do little to resolve the underlying problem in the country's security apparatus.

blocks.caption: Gibran Rakabuming Raka stepped down from his role as vice president this week [FILE: May 20, 2026]Image: Willy Kurniawan/REUTERS

blocks.text: The controversy has renewed calls for reforms that would prevent police surveillance capabilities from becoming instruments of political competition.
'Systematic abuse of power'

Because the latest wiretapping controversy targeted not only the president but also political elites and key civil society actors, "surveillance goes beyond mere politics," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta, told DW.
"It is a calculated and systematic abuse of power," he added.
Fahrizal argued that a fundamental problem lies in the National Police's constitutional and institutional position, which answers directly to the president.
This increases the risk that the police respond to presidential political interests rather than solely to the law.
In November last year, Prabowo established a police reform commission to investigate longstanding concerns about professionalism, governance, and accountability.
However, Fahrizal said former police chief Listyo failed to implement meaningful reforms, with the latest allegations showing the consequences of inadequate oversight.

Fahrizal called for Indonesia to bring its fragmented surveillance regulations together under a unified legal framework, with tighter controls over the interception powers of the police's Criminal Investigation Agency and the Intelligence and Security Agency.
"Internal police reform must urgently address this by restoring professionalism and a proper institutional ethos," Fahrizal said.
Without such changes, divided political loyalties risk becoming a "dangerous virus" spreading through the police and other security institutions, he added.

articles.title: Sara Duterte defense seen to end presentation within November: What next?
articles.summary: The pace at which the defense panel of Vice President Sara Duterte is presenting its witnesses in her impeachment trial makes it likely that it will finish presenting its case before the end of…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 10:03pm

The pace at which the defense panel of Vice President Sara Duterte is presenting its witnesses in her impeachment trial makes it likely that it will finish presenting its case before the end of November, the spokesman of the tribunal has said.

According to Sandra Aguinaldo's report on "24 Oras," the defense panel will have ten days to file its formal offer of evidence after it wraps up its presentation of witnesses. The prosecution will also have ten days to comment or file its opposition to the defense's case.

"Kung makikita natin sa bilis ng pagpepresenta ng mga witnesses po, ay nakaabot po tayo ng 3-4 witnesses in a day for the presentation for the defense. Ganun din po ‘yung ine-expect natin na time and motion na mangyayari sa mga succeeding hearing days,” Tongol said.

(Looking at the pace of the witness presentations, we have reached three to four witnesses a day for the defense's presentation. That is the same timeline and pace we expect to see in the succeeding hearing days.)
The court will then resolve on the formal offer and the comments within 10 days at most, according to the impeachment court spokesperson.
Verdict seen before Christmas
Atty. Paolo Panelo, Duterte’s spokesperson, explained why the Vice President’s camp expects the verdict to be handed down before the Christmas break.

“Ang sabi niya sa akin noon, ang parang pakay ng mga nagmamadali para habulin itong Christmas break ay para daw kung may conviction at magalit ‘yung mga tao, hindi sila makapag-express masyado ng galit nila dahil Pasko na at kung acquittal naman, eh di makakalimutan na sa susunod na taon, so ‘yun ang impormasyon na natanggap niya,” Panelo said.

(What she told me before was that the apparent motive of those rushing to beat the Christmas break is so that if there is a conviction and people get angry, they won't be able to express their outrage as much because it's already Christmas—and if it's an acquittal, it will simply be forgotten by next year. So that is the information she received.)
For its part, the prosecution said it also appears feasible to wrap up the impeachment proceedings before Christmas.

“We've been dwelling on this for three years already, and I think it's about time we put an end to this by witnessing the verdict as to whether it is conviction or acquittal at least before Christmas,” lead prosecutor Congressman Gerville Luistro said.
The next proceedings for Duterte’s impeachment trial are scheduled for November 19 to 20, after which the Senate will take a break from the trial to focus on the 2027 national budget.
The next trial day is expected to resume on December 1. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/NB, GMA News

articles.title: DepEd issues stronger work immersion guidelines for SHS students
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) on Friday said that it was strengthening its work immersion program for senior high school students by issuing renewed guidelines.

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 9:53pm
The Department of Education (DepEd) on Friday said that it was strengthening its work immersion program for senior high school students by issuing renewed guidelines.
This comes as the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) recorded a lower youth employment rate in September 2026. Many young workers have also reported that it was harder to look for more work.

“Ang work immersion ang makakapaghanda sa ating mga mag-aaral para mas maging job-ready sila, kaya mas malaki ang chance na agad makahanap ng trabaho ang graduates ng Grade 12,” DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara said in a statement.
(Work immersion prepares our students to be job-ready so there is a bigger chance for Grade 12 graduates to look for work.)

“May mga kausap na tayong partners sa industriya para sa mga guaranteed placement sa kanilang work immersion. Based on experience, the chances of employment are higher when they undergo a longer immersion period with the company or organization,” he added.

(We are speaking with partners in the industry so that there is guaranteed placement in their work immersion. Based on experience, the chances of employment are higher when they undergo a longer immersion period with the company or organization.)

DepEd Order No. 023, s. 2026 forms part of the Strengthened Senior High School (SSHS) Curriculum, and it aims to make practical learning more relevant to a learner’s chosen industry. Under the guidelines, work immersion is mandatory in the Technical-Professional (TechPro) Track.
TechPro students are required to undergo either a 320-hour one-term model or a 540- to 640-hour two-term model, depending on the school’s capacity.
Work immersion for learners in the Academic Track is still optional. Those who are interested, however, are allowed to undertake a 320-hour program after they complete their prerequisite electives.
Academic Track students may also take an 80-hour Field Exposure elective to explore possible career paths.
Arts Apprenticeship also allows students interested in creative fields to explore visual arts, media arts, performing arts, and more.
According to the DepEd, schools must assess and screen partner institutions and formalize agreements. Students must not be assigned tasks for free labor.
The work immersion activities must not surpass eight hours a day per day and five days a week, with the school being required to have regular check-in sessions with the students.
Aside from private companies, schools are also urged to partner with government units and agencies.

DepEd said that the guidelines will apply to public and private SSHS pilot implementers starting in the school year 2026-2027. The remaining senior high schools will implement the guidelines starting in 2027. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ASEAN Summit to tackle transnational crime, food security measures
articles.summary: As the Philippines wraps up its chairmanship of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, several key measures are expected to be finalized to address challenges facing member…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 9:45pm

As the Philippines wraps up its chairmanship of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, several key measures are expected to be finalized to address challenges facing member states.
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Friday said these measures aim to address issues including the impacts of the Middle East crisis, food security, and transnational crimes.

"Given the situation at the moment, we are still feeling the impacts of the Middle East crisis, so we should expect some additional measures and decisions from our leaders in addressing the energy situation that we're facing at the moment," Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Dominic Xavier "Dax" Imperial, spokesperson for ASEAN Affairs, said in a press briefing.
"We will also expect some decisions and measures with regard to more protection and welfare of migrant workers, especially the Filipino migrant workers," he added.

On November 14, DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro will convene the ASEAN foreign ministers for their final meeting, where they will review and decide on the implementation of the ASEAN Five-Point Consensus, as one of the agenda items.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will chair the ASEAN Summit and related summits from November 15 to 17.

The program on November 15 will start with an opening ceremony followed by the plenary and retreat sessions. It will culminate with the interface meetings with the ASEAN Interparliamentary Assembly, the ASEAN Business Advisory Council, and ASEAN youth.
The Plus One summits will be held from November 16-17.
On November 17, Marcos will convene the 29th ASEAN Plus Three Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Aide to fugitive Ukrainian ex-PM wounded in latest Moscow car bombing
articles.summary: Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was previously an adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov.

blocks.text: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.
Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was behind the wheel of his black Toyota when the explosion happened and Azarov told Russian TV his condition in hospital was "rather critical".

The car bomb went off a day after a Russian colonel was killed in another explosion in St Petersburg, and both blasts are seen as part of a series of attacks on military and prominent figures linked to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zavorotny, 72, worked as a press aide to Mykola Azarov in Kyiv until 2014.
But when pro-Kremlin Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled from power, Azarov fled Kyiv for Russia and tried unsuccessfully to set up a government in exile.

In a 2020 US Senate report on interference in the 2016 American presidential election, Zavorotny is described at the time as an SVR [Russian foreign intelligence] officer involved in influence operations.

Russia's Investigative Committee said on Telegram on Friday: "Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, was injured while driving a car. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care."
It added: "A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."
According to several unconfirmed reports, Zavorotny suffered a number of serious injuries after an explosive device was detonated remotely.
Russia said the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.
On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military, again after it was attached to the base of the car and detonated remotely.
The man targeted in the attack is yet to be named officially, but reputable sources suggest he was a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army.
Overnight into Friday, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.
Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.
They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.
Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.
And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.
Ukraine said these were retaliatory attacks in response to Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.

articles.title: Global Microsoft outage stretches into 2nd day

image.caption: People walk outside at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto on May 9, 2025. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

items: November 13Canadian hospitals, universities and government services impactedPeople walk outside at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto on May 9, 2025. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)In Canada, the outage has affected hospitals, universities, government departments and transportation services.Unity Health Toronto, which operates several hospitals including St. Michael's Hospital, declared a "code grey" on Thursday, indicating an infrastructure failure. The hospital network said staff were having difficulty sending and receiving emails, but patient care was not affected.Toronto's Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre and University Health Network also reported email disruptions.In Montreal, the CHUM hospital said the outage affected appointment requests and some internal activities. The Jewish General Hospital also said it was affected.Via Rail said some customers were not receiving emails about their trips and advised passengers to check its train tracker or sign up for text notifications.Several post-secondary institutions, including the University of Toronto, Seneca Polytechnic and George Brown Polytechnic, also reported email problems, although classes were expected to proceed as scheduled Friday.Some federal government departments and Toronto city hall also experienced email disruptions.-With files from CBC's Linda Ward

Microsoft outage affecting users in at least 74 countriesVerity StevensonA Microsoft Outlook logo seen on a laptop in Warsaw, Poland, amid an Outlook outage that has left users around the world without its crucial services. (Mladen Antonov/AFP/Getty Images)The outage has disrupted online services in at least 74 countries, according to online outage monitors.The disruption began around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. Microsoft 365 has more than 430 million paid users worldwide.The impacts appear to vary among users. Some report no issues, while others have been unable to send or receive emails or access virtual meetings.The Japanese government reported having issues, and Australia's intelligence agency also reported disruptions.In the United Kingdom, some health-care providers have been unable to share patient records between services. Airlines have also reported difficulties communicating with customers, while some businesses in Asia have struggled to receive orders.-WIth files from CBC's Julia Chapman

Microsoft outage disrupts services worldwide for second dayVerity StevensonA malfunctioning Microsoft Outlook website on a screen in Lausanne, Switzerland, on Friday. (Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images)A massive Microsoft outage is continuing to disrupt businesses, hospitals and government services around the world this morning, more than 12 hours after problems first emerged.The outage has affected services, including Outlook email, Teams and its AI assistant, Copilot, leaving users unable to send emails, access calendars or hold virtual meetings.The disruptions have been felt across Canada and in dozens of other countries, affecting everything from hospital communications to airline customer services and financial transactions.Microsoft says the outage was caused by server issues, with no indication of a cyberattack. The company says it is seeing signs of recovery, but services have yet to be fully restored.-With files from Reuters

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila

blocks.text: The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.
The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.
During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet, with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

image.caption: Anthropic is aiming for a valuation of more than $1 trillion when it goes public next weekImage: Carlos Barria/REUTERS

blocks.text: 2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves.
In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.
AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence.
Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters
AI doubts trigger market turbulence

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly.

Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged marital affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still.

blocks.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is under scrutiny over an affair with an alleged Chinese spyImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts.
In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "show me the money."
Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath
AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'

Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction."
"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO

While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share.
Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head. “Is this the best timing?” he asked.
While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion.
Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of over $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."
Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects.

“Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company,” Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. “Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.”
Signs to watch, not reasons to flee

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported last week.
"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."
That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.
Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers.

This summer, New York and Texas temporarily paused new data center approvals. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who takes office in January, wants new laws to stop data centers’ heavy power and water use from pushing up household bills.
Why US voters are fighting Trump's AI data center boom
Not 'different this time'

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railroads, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.
Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.
"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

articles.summary: Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself.

blocks.text: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?
The answer is very.

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.
Now the political pressure is building.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

articles.title: Iran says it destroyed US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and…

blocks.text: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain – its first direct attack on US military installations for months – in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump announced that he had asked his vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been in the forefront of Republicans saying the war led to the massive Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public, since higher diesel prices was a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

An opinion poll in the UK shows 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was found to be 45%, with 22% opposed.

The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.

Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”

Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.

In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for reviewing Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.

The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.

Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely inside political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.

The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
articles.summary: The Spanish singer is recognised for her fourth album Lux which was released last year to rave reviews.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews
ByRiyah Collins
BBC Newsbeat
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.
The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.
La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."
The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."
Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.
She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.
The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

blocks.caption: Image caption, After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement award

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement award
It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.
He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.
Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.
Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".
"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.
She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.
Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys

blocks.text: Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys
Accepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.
The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.
He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far".
"Long live Argentine folk music," he added.
Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.
Additional reporting by Abu Bakar Yasin

articles.title: What’s behind Australia’s surge in teen extremism?
articles.summary:
Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says

  • Get our

blocks.text: In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.
This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.

The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.

In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.
What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.
In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.

The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.
All matters are still before the courts.
Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.

Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.
She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.

“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”

The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks, reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.

A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.
Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse – is traded.

Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.
after newsletter promotion

It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.
“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.
With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.

The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.
Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.

There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.
“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.
“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”

articles.title: Van Hollen takes aim at Schumer as Democrats face first big test after midterms – US politics live
articles.summary:
Senator Van Hollen says midterm results show Americans want change in Washington, and Democrats need new leadership to deliver that

Good morning, and welcome to the US politics live…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 21m agoVan Hollen takes aim at Schumer as Democrats face first big test after midterm wins

blocks.text: Van Hollen takes aim at Schumer as Democrats face first big test after midterm wins
Good morning, and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Barely a week after sweeping to a stunning midterm victory, Democrats have found themselves facing an altogether different battle, one within their own ranks.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has launched a challenge to Chuck Schumer, of New York, for the Senate’s top Democratic leadership post. Announcing his decision during an interview with MS Now last night, Van Hollen argued that last week’s midterm election results showed Americans wanted a fundamental change in Washington, and that Democrats needed new leadership in order to deliver that.

blocks.caption: Chris Van Hollen said he is challenging Chuck Schumer to be Senate majority leader in the next Congress.  Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images

blocks.text: He said:

double quotation markWe saw a huge outburst of democracy on election day – red states, blue states, purple states – and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change, to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favour of the very wealthy against working people, and it’s fuelled by a corrupt political system. The call was to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

His challenge came just days after Democrats secured control of the Senate, winning at least 55 seats in what has been a remarkable election cycle for the party. Winning the leadership contest requires a majority of the caucus, about 28 or 29 senators, with an election scheduled for next month.
The caucus votes behind closed doors by secret ballot, but Van Hollen told MS Now that he had the support of “more than 10” Democratic senators.

Progressive heavyweight Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont who caucuses with the Democrats, has already publicly declared he will not support Schumer, saying “the time is now for change”. Endorsing Van Hollen, Sanders said: “The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”
Incoming Democratic senator Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, has also openly backed Van Hollen, saying he was “proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority”.

double quotation markThe American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called [Van Hollen] to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now.”

Responding to Van Hollen’s leadership bid, Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since January 2017, said he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”, but that he had the votes to be re-elected as leader.

articles.title: Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration
articles.summary: Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp says that midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in…

image.caption: Felix Nmecha has made 14 appearances for GermanyImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.
Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.
This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.
Nmecha 'does not discriminate against anyone'
​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.
"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.
"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."
He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

blocks.caption: Felix Nmecha's 'Crowns down' celebration caused much discussion over the past weekImage: Madeleine Fantini/HMB Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nations League quarterfinal berth up for grabs

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.
"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

blocks.caption: Jürgen Klopp is hoping to keep alive Germany's chances of a Nations League quarterfinal berthImage: Michael Memmler/nordphoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Just 5,000 children and coaches to attend

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.
"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

articles.title: They called her 'Mommy': Vulnerable senior dies after 2 strangers take over her life
articles.summary: Two men moved into an elderly Toronto woman's home and began claiming to be like her sons. She quickly gave them powers of attorney and signed a will, leaving them everything. Then she died.
articles.byline: Krista Hessey, Linda Guerriero, Ioanna Roumeliotis

image.caption: Elton John Rambarrat, left, and Daniel Gopie moved into Dorelia Licorish’s Toronto home and began calling her ‘Mommy.’ She signed a will leaving them everything, then she died. (llustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Photos: TikTok/Daniel Ram, Ousama Farag/CBC, Submitted by Carolyn Garner)

blocks.text: Dorelia Licorish didn't know where she was. Her confusion came after she was asked a simple question by a Toronto judge presiding over a video court hearing last May.
"Are you in Guyana right now?"
Licorish, an 86-year-old Toronto resident who was in the South American country at the time, turned to the two men with her.
"I'm supposed to say yes?"
"Yes," one of them responded.
A provincial agency had gone to court to get legal guardianship over Licorish, arguing she was mentally incapable and the men were taking advantage of her financially.
Back in Canada, members of her family had been searching for Licorish. They called police after they hadn't been able to reach her for weeks and her house looked abandoned.

Less than six months after that call, Licorish died in hospital from an infected bedsore so deep her pelvic bone was exposed. The two men with her in Guyana are living in her Toronto home. Police have laid no charges.
Licorish’s nieces, Susanne Perch, left, and Andrea Phillips-Beckles, right, are seeking answers from police about what happened to their aunt. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

An investigation by CBC's the fifth estate into Licorish's death reveals that even when government agencies and law enforcement are alerted to a case of suspected elder abuse, they can fail to protect the most vulnerable seniors.
Licorish's family believe she was neglected by the men who had moved in as tenants before declaring themselves her caregivers.
"I would like to get justice for her because [the police] didn't take anything seriously at all," said Andrea Phillips-Beckles, Licorish's niece.

items: Watch the full documentary, "The called her 'Mommy,'" from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: Mistreatment of older adults is on the rise, experts say, as Canada becomes a "super-aged" country this year, with one in five people aged 65 or older.

While rates of elder abuse are not tracked nationally, a 2022 study by University of Toronto researchers found one in 10 Canadians over age 65 experiences some form of elder abuse — physical, financial or sexual — every year, and racialized and cognitively impaired older adults are at higher risk.

"Dorelia's story is one that's being played out in so many places, among so many individuals each and every day in our country, and this issue is only growing bigger," said Dr. Samir Sinha, director of geriatrics at Sinai Health System and University Health Network in Toronto.
"What's preventing this from happening to you?"
An undated photo of Licorish. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
Beloved auntie

Licorish immigrated to Canada from Barbados in the early 1960s. She was sharp-witted and fiercely independent, her family and friends said. She did not have any children of her own, but after her sister died, raised Phillips-Beckles.
"She was one vibrant, vibrant woman," Phillips-Beckles said.
Licorish worked as a nurse at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health on Queen Street West in Toronto for decades before retiring.
Christiana Egi, Licorish's former nursing colleague and close friend of 35 years, told the fifth estate she noticed Licorish was displaying memory problems as early as 2018.
Remembering a much-loved family member
In early 2024, Licorish told Egi that a married couple, Daniel Gopie and Elton John Rambarrat, had moved into her basement and were helping her around the house.
"I was like, 'I hope this is for real, that something doesn't happen.'"
The first red flags for Licorish's family came in June 2024. Licorish's landline had been disconnected and a second cousin received word the new tenants had said the house was now in their name.
The cousin showed up at Licorish's home on Lawrence Avenue East with police, but Licorish got angry and asked them to leave.
Daniel Gopie, left, Licorish and Elton John Rambarrat in an undated photo. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

A month later, she gave Rambarrat and Gopie powers of attorney over her property and personal care — giving them control of her finances and health should she be deemed incapable. Then she signed a will leaving all her assets to them, including her million-dollar Toronto home.

When Phillips-Beckles went to the home in August 2024, she says Licorish didn't immediately recognize her and the men never left her aunt's side. One of the men told her Licorish's will is "bulletproof."
"He started calling her 'Mommy,' and then she said, 'These are my sons from God.' I said, 'No, they're sons from the devil,'" Phillips-Beckles said.
Legal documents in question
In September 2024, Ontario's Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee (OPGT) began looking into the relationship between Licorish and her tenants after receiving a tip from a real estate lawyer.
The OPGT is a provincial agency tasked with safeguarding the interests of mentally incapable Ontarians.
The lawyer told the agency he had been asked to add Rambarrat and Gopie to the title of Licorish's property. He refused after Licorish could not recall the men's names.

In a 120-page affidavit filed in Ontario Court of Justice, the OPGT detailed what allegedly happened after Rambarrat and Gopie moved in. The men said they had met Licorish at her church and she allowed them to live in the basement rent-free in exchange for helping her with shopping and chores.

They began going with Licorish to appointments with her longtime family doctor, court records show. The doctor told the OPGT that after an appointment in September 2024, she asked Licorish about the men and the powers of attorney document they had shown her, Licorish was "very surprised" and didn't remember signing it.
An undated photo of Gopie, left, Licorish and Rambarrat. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

Her family doctor wrote she had "concerns with Ms. Licorish's memory" and had booked a mini-mental status exam. However, Rambarrat cancelled the appointment. In medical notes from August 2025, doctors wrote Licorish had a history of dementia but it is unclear when it was first diagnosed.
In an interview with the fifth estate, the men said Licorish did not have dementia and was capable of granting them powers of attorney and creating a will that named them sole beneficiaries.
"The lawyer did the will. She did think it was fine and we didn't see it as a problem; it's something [Licorish] wanted to do," Rambarrat said.
The lawyer, Veena Pohani, told OPGT that while the three had "an unconventional relationship," she did not see signs of abuse and Licorish appeared happy.
Pohani declined to be interviewed for this story, citing client-solicitor privilege.
Rambarrat says lawyer Veena Pohani created the powers of attorney documents and will for Licorish. (veenapohani.com)

While a dementia diagnosis does not necessarily mean someone is incapable, lawyers have a duty to ensure clients have the mental capacity to understand the legal decisions they are making and that they are not being pressured by outside forces, according to the Ontario Law Society.
Pohani told the OPGT Licorish was capable of making these decisions, although no information is included about how she determined that.
Allegations of financial abuse

Banking records submitted in court show a dramatic change in Licorish's spending around the time the men entered her life. Thousands of dollars in ATM cash withdrawals and near-weekly alcohol purchases quickly depleted her modest pension and drove her account into overdraft.

Rambarrat and Gopie were added to Licorish's accounts in early October 2024. They cashed out some of her investments and withdrew money from her line of credit a few weeks before they took Licorish to their home country of Guyana for the first time.
Undated photos of Licorish with Gopie and Rambarrat in Guyana. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)
Bank staff wrote to OPGT that Licorish told them she "trusts them fully" and the transactions were completed with her consent.
However, about six weeks later, Licorish told OPGT investigators that she was not aware of withdrawals in the thousands.
Rambarrat and Gopie deny using Licorish's money for their own purposes and say they used it for home repairs.
However, when asked by OPGT investigators, they could not provide a receipt.
Family tries to intervene
Over 18 months, Licorish's family members made multiple calls to Toronto police, voicing concerns about the men's relationship with their elderly relative.
Body camera recordings and records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act show police treated multiple reports as "family disputes."
The fifth estate also learned police went to Licorish's house in March 2024, the same month the men allegedly moved in, and noticed she had cognitive issues.

items: Rising number of cases of senior abuse and neglect point to needed changes, says B.C. seniors advocate
Family violence against seniors reaches record high in Canada: StatsCan

blocks.text: Court records also reveal Gopie, who became Licorish's main caregiver, pleaded guilty to two assault charges in 2013 and 2018, unrelated to Licorish. Yet, police took no action to intervene.
Retired Durham police detective Martin Franssen, who specialized in suspected cases of elder abuse and reviewed the OPGT court file, says Licorish's case is "textbook."
He says Gopie's criminal history and Licorish's vulnerable mental state should have alerted officers to look into the situation more.
"This is the future of Canada — based on the changing age demographics — and we have to change our ways."
OPGT goes to court, Licorish goes to Guyana
In October 2024, the OPGT filed a notice in court to remove Rambarrat and Gopie as Licorish's powers of attorney for property and for the agency to take over her financial affairs.
However, seven months passed before OPGT submitted evidence.
By then, the men had taken Licorish to Guyana for a second time. All three attended a virtual court hearing to assign Licorish a lawyer who would be tasked with discerning her wishes.
In the audio recording of the hearing, obtained by the fifth estate, the OPGT's lawyer said the agency went to court "hastily" and did more investigative work after speaking to Pohani.
The lot in New Amsterdam, Guyana, where sources say Rambarrat and Gopie intend to build a house. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
The men told the judge they were in Guyana because they are building a house. They said they brought Licorish with them because they were her caregivers and it wasn't safe for her to be left alone.
The men spoke for Licorish until the judge asked if there was anything she wanted to say.
"I don't want them to leave me," she replied weakly.

Franssen says it is common in predatory relationships involving older adults for the perpetrator to quickly make the victim feel dependent upon them, making it less likely that they will report the abuse.
"If cognition comes into play … they may not even realize it's being done, but they will believe, in a lot of cases I've seen and dealt with, that they have that reliance on that individual."
The fifth estate spoke to several residents who saw and interacted with Licorish while she was in Guyana. Fearing retaliation, CBC News agreed not to identify them.

Multiple sources questioned how well Licorish was being cared for because Gopie would drink heavily, sometimes becoming intoxicated with Licorish. They said the three of them stayed in a dilapidated home where several other people connected to Rambarrat also lived.
Sources say the men and Licorish stayed at this house for weeks alongside several other members of Rambarrat’s family. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
During the trip, Licorish grew too weak to leave the house independently and would be left alone for hours, several sources said.
The men deny this, saying she was on vacation and well-cared for. They say she only visited the rundown home during the day and slept elsewhere.

The fifth estate has learned that when Licorish returned to Canada in July 2025, the lawyer assigned to her at the court hearing was unable to obtain instructions, though there was no explanation as to why.
"We have a system that, as designed, can't act quickly enough," Sinha said. "We don't have the luxury of time in these cases."
Licorish's final months

Upon returning from Guyana, Licorish's mental and physical health had declined, Licorish's friends and family said. She became bedridden after a brief hospitalization in August for a swollen knee and began receiving visits from personal support workers and nurses.

Partial records from the province's home-care agency, Ontario Health atHome, obtained by the fifth estate show Licorish had a pressure injury on her tailbone on Oct. 5, 2025. Nursing notes say the men were not "willing and able" to care for the wound.
The Victorian Order of Nurses, a non-profit nursing agency, was authorized to send someone to tend to the bedsore every three days.

A nurse reported to Ontario Health atHome Rambarrat had assisted him with turning Licorish because she would not allow the male nurse to touch her and he advised Rambarrat to turn Licorish frequently.
That same nurse said on Nov. 5 he requested a specialist to come to look at the wound because it was getting bigger and deeper. However, it's unclear if that occurred.
Licorish was unresponsive when she arrived at Scarborough General Hospital on Nov. 7, 2025. (Submitted by Susanne Perch)
On Nov. 7, 2025, Licorish was rushed to Scarborough General Hospital after a nurse found her unresponsive, medical records show.

She had gone into septic shock, a reaction to an infected Stage 4 bedsore, the most severe rating, that was oozing brown liquid and had a foul smell. Doctors also noted "profound dehydration" and high blood sugar levels.
When asked why he or Gopie did not take Licorish to the hospital sooner, Rambarrat said they deferred to the health-care professionals caring for Licorish.
Both S.R.T.-Med-Staff, the agency sending PSWs to care for Licorish daily, and the Victorian Order of Nurses did not respond to detailed questions, citing privacy laws.
The men, as Licorish's attorneys for personal care, had a legal duty of care to her, retired police detective Franssen said.
"Why didn't you pick up [and call] 911? Why did you need a health-care professional to walk in that day and turn to you and say, 'I suggest you call 911?'"
Licorish died on Nov. 21, 2025, 10 days after the men agreed for her to be moved to palliative care.
Sinha says her death was preventable.
"If she arrived at the hospital sooner, she may still be alive."
Because of her passing, the OPGT's case in court was dismissed.
Police close the case

Licorish's family only found out she was in hospital after a cousin driving by her house saw an ambulance out front. When they became aware of Licorish's condition, they called Toronto police again. This time, they alleged the men neglected Licorish and begged police to investigate.
In May, six months after Licorish's death, Toronto police detectives informed the family they had closed the case.
Toronto police declined interview requests, saying in a statement they conducted a thorough review of the circumstances surrounding Licorish's care, finances and death.

"The investigation included the examination of extensive medical, home care and other records, consultation with multiple parties involved in her care.... Following that investigation, no evidence was identified to support the laying of criminal charges," a media spokesperson wrote.

Multiple members of Licorish's extended family called Toronto Police Service's 43 Division about Rambarrat and Gopie's relationship with their elderly aunt. They accuse the police of not taking their concerns seriously. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Family members are in the process of contesting Licorish's will, arguing she wasn't mentally capable at the time of signing.
Rambarrat and Gopie say Licorish's family did not care for her and they are entitled to her house.
"I'm obligated to get something," Gopie said in an interview. "Does nobody come and clean her piss? Clean her shit? Do anything for her?"
Phillips-Beckles has a binder of files and contacts she's been collecting as she tries to piece together what happened to her aunt.
"I can't wrap my head around it at all, that she's gone and how she went," she said. "She shouldn't have gone that way."
